Record date: 2130-01-27
South Elizabeth Seychelles Hospital INTERNAL MEDICINE DEPARTMENT Location: 4923 Olivia Parkway Suite 217, Lake Jennabury
PATIENT: Lysander Fairfax Phone: 28451903 email:bradleymorgan@example.org DATE OF BIRTH: 1947-05-12 AGE: 80 years
FOLLOW-UP DATE: 01/27/30 FOLLOWED BY: Dr. Emily Carter
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Persistent shortness of breath and cough with increased sputum production despite recent antibiotic therapy.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Lysander Fairfax returns for a follow-up visit two days post initiation of oral Levofloxacin for his COPD exacerbation and pneumonia. He reports minimal improvement in his respiratory symptoms, noting that his cough remains productive with yellowish-green sputum. The patient continues to experience significant dyspnea, particularly during activities of daily living, and reports that his fatigue persists, severely limiting his ability to engage in usual activities.
Despite adherence to his prescribed medications, Mr. Fairfax states that he has experienced intermittent fevers, with temperatures fluctuating between 99F and 100.8F, and reports ongoing night sweats. He expresses frustration regarding the persistent mild epigastric discomfort, which he describes as a dull ache, and states that the heartburn has not improved despite Omeprazole therapy.
REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General - + persistent fatigue, + intermittent fevers, + night sweats, - weight loss. Pulmonary - + persistent productive cough with yellowish-green sputum, + significant dyspnea, + wheezing, - hemoptysis. Cardiac - no chest pain, - orthopnea, - paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Gastrointestinal - + mild epigastric discomfort, + heartburn, - nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Musculoskeletal - no joint pain. Neurological - no dizziness or headaches.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: - Blood Pressure: 130/82 mmHg - Heart Rate: 90 bpm - Respiratory Rate: 30 breaths/min - Oxygen Saturation: 82% on supplemental oxygen (6 L via nasal cannula).
General: The patient appears fatigued and is in moderate respiratory distress, exhibiting use of accessory muscles for breathing.
HEENT: No nasal flaring; oropharynx clear, no signs of dehydration.
Lungs: Significant wheezing on auscultation; diminished breath sounds bilaterally; prolonged expiration with rhonchi; audible crackles throughout lung fields, particularly in the lower lobes.
Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs or gallops; peripheral pulses intact.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender; mild epigastric discomfort noted; no hepatosplenomegaly.
ASSESSMENT
1. Persistent chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation with ongoing bacterial pneumonia, indicated by unchanged respiratory symptoms and continued hypoxemia despite treatment. 2. Inadequate response to current antibiotic therapy; potential need for adjustment based on clinical status and sputum culture results. 3. Fatigue likely exacerbated by ongoing respiratory compromise and systemic steroid therapy; gastrointestinal symptoms persist, warranting further evaluation.
PLAN
1. Obtain a sputum culture and sensitivity test to identify the causative organism; consider broadening antibiotic therapy to include intravenous Ceftriaxone 1 g every 24 hours if there is no improvement in 48 hours. 2. Continue oral Prednisone at 60 mg daily, with plans to taper based on clinical response; continue Omeprazole 20 mg daily to manage gastric irritation. 3. Increase supplemental oxygen to 8 L via nasal cannula; consider the initiation of BiPAP therapy if there is no significant improvement in oxygen saturation or if the patient's respiratory distress escalates. 4. Schedule a repeat chest X-ray today to evaluate for any progression of pneumonia; assess for potential pleural effusion or other complications. 5. Continue nebulized bronchodilator therapy (Albuterol) every four hours as needed; consider adding Ipratropium bromide to enhance bronchodilation. 6. Schedule a follow-up visit within 48 hours to reassess respiratory status and medication efficacy; discuss the potential for pulmonary rehabilitation once stabilized.
DISPOSITION
Mr. Fairfax remains under close observation in the internal medicine unit. The treatment team will continue to modify the management plan based on his clinical progress, particularly focusing on his respiratory function and gastrointestinal symptoms. Patient education regarding the importance of adherence to the new antibiotic regimen and the need to report any new or worsening symptoms will be emphasized during this visit.
